_note: Frozen content for design review. Mono family — the voice is earned because the subject is command-line tools. Every page shows the same transform: what goes in, what acts, what comes out.
brief: Six command-line tools that removed a step each

slots.eyebrow: Six replacements, one afternoon to install
slots.subtitle: Six drop-in replacements for commands you type every day. Each one removes a wait rather than adding a capability.
slots.v1: replaced by a search that skips what git ignores
slots.v2: replaced by a viewer that shows syntax and line numbers
slots.v3: replaced by a matcher that reads the same ignore rules
slots.v4: replaced by a filter you type into instead of scroll
slots.coverNote: Everything below is a single install command

slots.body: It reads your ignore files by default, so a search across a repository never descends into dependencies or build output. That single default is most of the speed difference.
slots.flowIn: a string, somewhere in the repository
slots.flowAct: rg searches only the tracked files
slots.flowOut: matches, with paths and line numbers
slots.note1Body: Finding where something is used before you change it.
slots.note2Body: It honours ignore rules, so anything deliberately ignored stays invisible.

slots.body: It takes lines on standard input and returns the one you chose, which means every list you already produce becomes selectable without writing anything new.
slots.flowIn: any list of lines on standard input
slots.flowOut: the one line you picked, on standard output
slots.note1Body: Branches, history, files, and anything you were about to copy by hand.
slots.note2Body: It is only as good as the list you pipe into it, which is where the work is.

slots.body: Syntax highlighting, line numbers and the git status of each line, which turns reading a file in the terminal from a dump into something you can navigate.
slots.flowIn: a file you want to read, not edit
slots.flowAct: bat renders it with syntax and line numbers
slots.flowOut: a page you can actually scan
slots.note1Body: Checking a config or a script before you run it.
slots.note2Body: It pages by default, which breaks scripts that expected raw output.

slots.body: The common case is finding a file by part of its name, and that case takes one word rather than four flags. Everything else is still there when you need it.
slots.flowIn: part of a filename you half remember
slots.flowAct: fd walks the tree, ignoring what git ignores
slots.note1Body: The nine times in ten when you only know part of the name.
slots.note2Body: Different flags from find, so muscle memory fights you for a week.

slots.body: Structured output stops being something you squint at and becomes something you query, which is the difference between checking an API response and understanding it.
slots.flowIn: a response nobody wants to read
slots.flowAct: jq selects the fields that matter
slots.flowOut: the two values you were looking for
slots.note1Body: Any command that already speaks structured output.
slots.note2Body: It is a language, not a flag, and the first hour feels like a bad trade.

slots.body: Every one of these is an install away on your laptop and absent from the server you will be debugging at three in the morning. The old commands are the ones that are always there.
slots.flowIn: a habit built on tools you installed
slots.flowAct: a server with none of them
slots.note1Body: Local work, where you control what is installed.
slots.note2Body: Keep enough of the originals to survive a bare machine.

slots.eyebrow: One command, then use it for a week
slots.body: Pick the command you type most and swap only that one. A week of using it is the only test that tells you whether the habit sticks.
slots.flowIn: the command you type most often
slots.flowOut: a week of evidence instead of an opinion
slots.signoff: The other five keep until this one sticks
slots.closingLine: A tool you installed and never typed again cost you nothing but the evening.
